title: Why You Need a Lesson Observation Methodology
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that most schools carry out evaluative lesson observations from established habit rather than a defensible methodology, and that this gap matters because the research evidence on observer reliability is weak. Drawing on Rob Coe's synthesis of the evidence, he lays out five reasons untrained observers routinely disagree with each other and are often wrong even when they do agree. Hart's core claim is that improving observation quality requires deliberate, trained methodology rather than more observation itself, and he sketches ten components such a methodology should include -- from a stated purpose and shared framework for great teaching through to moderation, triangulation, and a defined feedback and action process. The piece closes by tying the argument to professional legitimacy: other high-stakes professions do not leave consequential judgements to individual impression, and schools should not either. It functions as a setup post for a forthcoming worked example and decision grid.
points: Hart's central claim is that lesson observation quality is a training and methodology problem, not a matter of experience or good intentions, citing Rob Coe's finding that untrained observers show only modest agreement and are often wrong even when they agree.

He distinguishes developmental observation (for teacher improvement) from evaluative observation (for judging teaching quality across a school), arguing both are legitimate but require different approaches and that clarity about which one is happening is a precondition for doing either well.

The proposed ten-part methodology (purpose, shared framework, observer requirements, frequency/notice, evidence recording, moderation, triangulation, unit of interest, feedback process, action requirement) reframes observation as a data-collection process requiring the same rigor as other professional judgements.

Hart's argument that 'we assume that if you can do it you can spot it' names a specific, common leadership blind spot: competence at teaching does not transfer automatically to competence at evaluating teaching.
The piece positions moderation and triangulation as non-negotiable safeguards against a single observer's judgement standing in for the reality of teaching quality in a school.
quotes: We all have established practices for lesson observations but we might not have a methodology.

...when untrained observers are asked to judge the quality of a lesson, there is likely to be only modest agreement among them. Worse still, even if they do agree that what they see is good practice, it often actually isn't.

School leaders are not typically formally trained in observing lessons. Some schools might put on in house observation training, but this can still simply magnify some of Coe's reasons for unreliability.

When we do not have a methodology, what gets noticed in a lesson depends on who is watching. Two observers in the same room will see different things, value different things and feed back different things.

Without a methodology that specifies what observers need to know and how they are trained, observation defaults to what is most visible; the pace of the lesson, whether students appear busy, whether the teacher seems confident.

A single observation by a single observer is not enough. Without multiple observations, multiple observers, agreed criteria, independent recording and a moderation process, the judgement is more likely to reflect the observer's preferences than the reality of teaching in the school.
Other professions don't leave high stakes judgements to individual impression and neither should we.
